notes: Ruling slot 23 = Trucial States Council (the seven hereditary rulers). Royal houses spread by orientation: Al Nahyan in 0 as in MD (with sprite), Al Maktoum in 1, Al Qasimi (Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah) in 13, the rulers of Ajman, Umm al-Quwain and Fujairah as a bloc in 14. Deposed rulers' followings: Shakhbut of Abu Dhabi in 6 (conservative), Saqr bin Sultan of Sharjah in 7 (Nasserist, Cairo exile). Trucial Oman Scouts in 22 as precursor of MD's UAE Armed Forces; Ba'ath in 21 as in MD; Muslim Brotherhood network in 12 (Al-Islah not founded until 1974). PFLOAG in 5, NDFLOAG in 19, ANM in 18.

0.name: Al Nahyan
0.text:
The Al Nahyan, of the Bani Yas, rule Abu Dhabi, the largest and richest of the Trucial States. Shaikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan took power in August 1966 when his brother Shakhbut was deposed with British approval, and has since poured oil revenues into roads, schools, housing and a fast-growing defence force officered by Britons and other foreigners.

Zayed aims to build a federation of the emirates with Abu Dhabi at its centre, keep British and Western friendship after 1971 and settle the Saudi claim to Buraimi and the western desert. He governs paternally through the majlis, generosity and tribal ties. His leverage is Abu Dhabi's oil wealth, which already bankrolls much of the coast's development.

1.name: Al Maktoum
1.text:
The Al Maktoum have ruled Dubai since 1833, when they broke away from Abu Dhabi with a branch of the Bani Yas. Shaikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum, Ruler since 1958, has made his town the commercial capital of the coast: he dredged the Creek, opened an airport and is building a deep-water port, and Dubai's first oil exports from the Fateh field began in 1969.

Rashid's Dubai stands for business, low taxes, free trade and pragmatic friendship with Britain, Iran and India alike. He favours a federation that respects Dubai's autonomy and its partnership with Abu Dhabi agreed in 1968. His leverage is wealth, commerce and the confidence of a merchant community that sees him as one of its own.

2.name: Jil al-Khirrijin
2.text:
The Graduates' Generation are the first Emiratis to have studied in Kuwait, Cairo, Baghdad, Beirut and Britain, now returning to staff the new administrations of Abu Dhabi and Dubai, the schools and the Trucial States Development Office. Among them is Ahmed Khalifa al-Suwaidi, head of the Abu Dhabi Ruler's Diwan and one of Zayed's chief negotiators in the federation talks.

They want a strong federal union with a written constitution, common institutions, modern education and health services, and gradual popular participation instead of rule by seven separate courts. They admire Kuwait and Arab nationalism but are reformers, not revolutionaries. Their leverage is that the emirates cannot build a modern state without their skills.

3.name: Maktab al-Kuwayt
3.text:
The Kuwait Office is the local arm of Kuwait's General Authority for the South and the Arabian Gulf, which since the 1950s has built and run schools, clinics and hospitals in Dubai, Sharjah and the northern emirates, staffed by teachers and doctors on Kuwaiti salaries. For thousands of families it, not the British, is the face of a modern state.

Its officials and the teachers it employs promote the Kuwaiti model: free public education and health care, salaried jobs, Arab cultural identity and a welfare state financed by oil. That model carries a quietly Arab nationalist message which the British watch with suspicion. Its leverage lies in classrooms, clinics and the gratitude of the poorer emirates.

4.name: Al-Khalaya al-Hamra'
4.text:
The Red Cells are a handful of Moscow-oriented communists among the Iraqi, Bahraini, Palestinian and Iranian teachers, clerks and dock workers of Dubai and Sharjah. They keep contact with Bahrain's National Liberation Front and the Iraqi Communist Party, meet in private homes and are watched by the British-officered police forces of the coast.

They call for the end of British protection, nationalisation of oil, a democratic republic uniting the emirates, legal trade unions and friendship with the Soviet Union. They regard the federation of rulers as a British device and the guerrilla left as adventurist. Their leverage is minimal but persistent: literature, workplace grievances and a long patience.

5.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-'Arabi al-Muhtall
5.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arab Gulf
5.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-'Arabi al-Muhtall
5.text:
The Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arab Gulf, the Marxist movement born of the Dhofar rebellion, regards the Trucial States as part of the colonial order it means to overthrow. Since its Hamrin congress of 1968 it has recruited former Arab Nationalist Movement members among Emirati students and teachers and among Omani migrant workers on the coast.

It rejects the planned federation as a British device to keep the shaikhs in place after withdrawal, and calls for people's war, the expulsion of foreign bases and oil companies and a socialist Gulf republic. It is armed and trained via South Yemen and inspired by China. On the coast its leverage lies in migrant networks, schools and arms smuggled along the Omani frontier.
5.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Oman

6.name: Rijal Shakhbut
6.text:
Shakhbut's Men are the old guard of Abu Dhabi loyal to Shaikh Shakhbut bin Sultan Al Nahyan, who ruled from 1928 until his brother Zayed replaced him in August 1966 with British backing. Shakhbut distrusted the oil companies, banks and foreign advisers, and his supporters among older tribesmen and retainers have never forgiven London for his removal.

They stand for the austere desert way of life, the authority of the shaikh over strangers, suspicion of Western contractors, foreign workers and lavish spending, and an end to British meddling in the succession of rulers. They want no part of modern parties or plans. Their leverage is small but symbolic: the living former Ruler as a reproach to the new order.

7.name: Ansar Saqr bin Sultan
7.text:
Saqr bin Sultan's Partisans are the supporters of Shaikh Saqr bin Sultan Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah until June 1965, when the British had him deposed after he welcomed the Arab League's plans for the Trucial States. Since then he has lived in exile in Cairo under Nasser's protection, while relatives, retainers and Arab nationalists in Sharjah keep his cause alive.

They want the British out, an Arab League presence on the coast, a federation tied to Cairo rather than London and Saqr restored to power. Their model is a strong Arab nationalist ruler backed by Egypt rather than by treaties with Britain. Their leverage lies in Egyptian support, family claims in Sharjah and popular resentment of British interference.

8.name: Al-Shiraziyyun
8.text:
The Shirazis are the followers on the Trucial coast of Grand Ayatollah Muhammad al-Shirazi of Karbala, whose representatives serve the Shia families of Iranian and Bahraini origin in Dubai, Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. They gather in husayniyyas and merchant majlises, where young men are drawn into study circles that present Islam as a programme for action.

They ask for freedom of worship, Shia religious courts and endowments, equal treatment in the emerging state and a moral order guided by the clergy. They avoid open clashes with the rulers, on whose favour the Shia merchants depend. Their leverage lies in the commercial wealth of the community and its connections with Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq and Iran.

9.name: Muqallidu al-Khumayni
9.text:
Khomeini's Followers are a small group of Shia on the Trucial coast, many of Iranian origin, who follow Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965, rather than the quietist senior clergy. They circulate his writings, pass his rulings among the faithful and help his emissaries travelling between Iraq, Kuwait and Iran.

They denounce the Shah as a tyrant allied to America and Israel and hold that the clergy, not kings, should govern Muslims. In the emirates they keep a low profile; their real target is the Pahlavi regime across the water, which they hope to see swept away. Their leverage lies in fervour and in a network that spans the Gulf.

10.name: Ansar al-Riyadh
10.text:
Riyadh's Partisans are the Na'im and Al Bu Shamis notables of the Buraimi oasis and the Wahhabi-minded scholars of the coast who look to Saudi Arabia as the protector of true religion. Many of their kinsmen sided with the Saudi occupation of Hamasa in 1952 and followed its garrison into exile in 1955, and Riyadh still claims much of Abu Dhabi's territory.

They want Saudi tutelage over the emirates, strict Wahhabi practice, stern Shari'a courts and an end to the influence of Western contractors, Shia merchants and Arab socialists. They see King Faisal as the natural overlord of the peninsula. Their leverage is Saudi money and the unresolved border dispute, which gives Riyadh a say over any federation.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, has reached the Trucial coast through Jordanian and Palestinian teachers and clerks working in Dubai, Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. Its tiny secret circles meet for study and distribute leaflets attacking the rulers, the British and the Arab nationalists alike.

The party holds that the emirates, like every Muslim state today, are illegitimate, and that a single caliph must reunite the Islamic world under Shari'a once power is handed over by those who hold it. It rejects federation, democracy and both superpowers. Its leverage is ideological conviction rather than numbers or arms.

12.name: Al-Ikhwan al-Muslimun
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood has no organisation of its own on the Trucial coast, but its ideas arrive with the Egyptian, Kuwaiti and other Arab teachers who staff the schools of Dubai, Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah, and with the first Emirati students returning from Cairo and Kuwait, where many met the Brothers. Kuwait's Social Reform Society serves as its model and patron.

The Brothers want Islamic education, moral reform, charity and mosques for a society transformed by oil, and they oppose secular Arab nationalism, communism and Western permissiveness alike. They prefer working with the rulers to confronting them. Their leverage lies in the classroom and in the trust of pious families anxious about rapid change.

13.name: Al-Qawasim
13.text:
The Al Qasimi, once a maritime power whose fleets the British destroyed in 1819, rule both Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah. In Ras al-Khaimah Shaikh Saqr bin Muhammad Al Qasimi has reigned since 1948 and is searching for oil of his own; in Sharjah his kinsman Shaikh Khalid bin Muhammad Al Qasimi has ruled since 1965, when the British removed his predecessor.

The Qawasim guard their dynastic prestige and separate statehood, demand equal weight with Abu Dhabi and Dubai in any federation and defend their claims to Abu Musa and the Tunbs against Iran. Saqr in particular keeps his options open with Arab capitals beyond Britain's reach. Their leverage lies in history, population and the islands question.

14.name: Al-Imarat al-Sughra
14.text:
The Small Emirates are the three poorest shaikhdoms of the coast and their ruling families: Ajman under Shaikh Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi, Umm al-Quwain under Shaikh Ahmad bin Rashid Al Mualla and Fujairah under Shaikh Muhammad bin Hamad Al Sharqi. Without oil, they live from fishing, date gardens, customs fees, postage stamps and subsidies from richer neighbours.

They want a federation in which each emirate keeps an equal voice, its own ruler and its own customs, while development money flows from Abu Dhabi and abroad. They are conservative, tribal and loyal to the British connection as long as it pays. Their leverage lies in their votes in the Trucial States Council and in the federation talks.

15.name: Ghurfat Tijarat wa-Sina'at Dubayy
15.english: Dubai Chamber of Commerce and Industry
15.text:
The Dubai Chamber of Commerce and Industry, founded in 1965, brings together the merchant houses that have made the Creek the busiest market of the lower Gulf, among them the Al Futtaim, Al Ghurair and Galadari families as well as long-established Indian and Iranian traders. Its members hold the agencies for Western cars, electrical goods and building materials.

The Chamber wants an open port, minimal taxation, a stable currency, a federal customs regime that does not cripple Dubai's re-export trade and continued good relations with Britain, Iran and India. It distrusts radicals and bureaucratic planners alike. Its leverage lies in capital, credit and its close partnership with Shaikh Rashid, who governs Dubai much like a chairman of the board.

16.name: Tujjar al-Dhahab
16.text:
The Gold Traders are the bullion dealers, financiers and dhow owners of Dubai who buy gold legally in London and Switzerland and ship it, quite openly from Dubai's side, to the Indian and Pakistani coasts where its import is banned. Their trade has filled Dubai's banks and suq with money and binds Arab, Indian and Iranian partners in a tight commercial network.

They want no customs on transit, no exchange controls, no questions about destinations and a federation that leaves Dubai's free-port regime untouched. Any state intervention or international pressure threatens their profits. Their leverage lies in the hard cash they put into Dubai's economy and in their influence with the Ruler.

17.name: Ahl al-Aflaj
17.text:
The Keepers of the Aflaj are the farmers, falaj wardens and village elders of the Al Ain and Buraimi oases, Liwa and the mountain valleys of Ras al-Khaimah and Fujairah, whose date gardens depend on ancient underground water channels. As diesel pumps and new wells multiply, they watch the water table fall and old channels run dry.

They demand careful management of groundwater, protection of the falaj system, tree planting and controls on overgrazing and uncontrolled hunting in the desert, a cause Shaikh Zayed himself has embraced in Al Ain. Their outlook is rooted in custom more than ideology. Their leverage is moral and local: the oases are the heartland of tribal identity.

18.name: Harakat al-Qawmiyyin al-'Arab
18.text:
The Arab Nationalist Movement, founded in Beirut in the early 1950s around George Habash, built its first cells on the Trucial coast among teachers, clerks and students in Dubai, Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah during the 1960s. Since the movement broke into national branches in 1968-69, its local circles are divided between Nasserist loyalists and militants drifting towards the Gulf liberation fronts.

Its Nasserist core wants a single Arab Gulf state free of British protection, Arab socialist development, Arabisation of schools and administration and solidarity with Egypt and the Palestinian revolution. It is hostile to Iranian claims and Western oil interests. Its leverage lies in youth clubs, schools and the respect it enjoys among educated Emiratis.

19.name: Al-Jabha al-Wataniyya al-Dimuqratiyya li-Tahrir 'Uman wa-l-Khalij
19.english: National Democratic Front for the Liberation of Oman and the Arab Gulf
19.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Wataniyya al-Dimuqratiyya li-Tahrir 'Uman wa-l-Khalij al-'Arabi
19.text:
Formed in 1969 by Arab Nationalist Movement veterans and other militants from inner Oman and the Trucial coast, the National Democratic Front works clandestinely to open a northern front against the Sultan of Muscat and the British-protected shaikhs, complementing the war in Dhofar. Its cells move between the coastal towns and the Omani interior, gathering arms and recruits.

It calls for a national democratic revolution in Oman and the Gulf, uniting workers, peasants and tribesmen against the sultan, the shaikhs and imperialism, and keeps its own counsel between Moscow and Beijing while learning from both. It prefers small urban and mountain cells to a mass movement. Its leverage lies in migrant networks, arms smuggling and the example of Dhofar.

20.name: Hurras al-Juzur
20.text:
The Guardians of the Islands are the young men of Ras al-Khaimah, Sharjah and the coastal towns who rally to defend Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs against Iran's claims, now that Britain's coming departure has reopened the question. They organise through sports and cultural clubs, write slogans on walls and press the rulers never to bargain away Arab land.

Their populism mixes Arab pride with resentment of the Iranian and South Asian immigrants who dominate trade and labour in the towns. They demand jobs for nationals, curbs on immigration and Arabic in public life. Their leverage is street feeling on an issue on which no ruler can afford to look weak.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
Ba'athist cells on the Trucial coast are recent and small, recruited among Iraqi, Syrian and Palestinian teachers and a few Emirati students who studied in Baghdad. Since the Iraqi Ba'ath took power in July 1968, Baghdad has offered scholarships and propaganda to win the coast's youth away from Britain and Iran.

The party preaches Arab unity, freedom and socialism under a vanguard party, the end of the separate shaikhdoms and of British bases, and defence of the islands against Iran. It is hostile to the Shah, to Zionism and to its communist rivals. Its leverage lies in Iraqi patronage and in Arab nationalist anger over the islands.

22.name: Trucial Oman Scouts
22.text:
The Trucial Oman Scouts, raised by the British in 1951 as the Trucial Oman Levies and headquartered in Sharjah, are the only force serving all seven emirates. British officers command Arab, Baluch and Omani soldiers who patrol the desert, guard the oil companies, settle tribal disputes and in 1955 helped drive the Saudis out of Buraimi.

With British withdrawal approaching, the Scouts expect to become the army of the future federation, and their officers favour a unified command, professional standards and strong ties to Britain. They are wary of the rulers' private armies, above all Abu Dhabi's. Their leverage is that no ruler can secure his frontiers or his throne without them.

23.name: Majlis al-Imarat al-Mutasaliha
23.text:
The Trucial States Council was created by the British in 1952 to bring the Trucial rulers together, and since 1965 it has been chaired by the rulers themselves and has run its own development fund and office. Its members are Zayed of Abu Dhabi, Rashid of Dubai, Khalid of Sharjah, Saqr of Ras al-Khaimah, Rashid of Ajman, Ahmad of Umm al-Quwain and Muhammad of Fujairah.

The Council stands for hereditary rule by consensus of the ruling families, under British protection until 1971 and in a federation thereafter, though talks on a nine-member union with Bahrain and Qatar stalled in October 1969. Its rulers agree on little beyond preserving their own authority. Its leverage is that every decision about the coast's future must pass through it.
